newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Black Point delay could cost over HK$1.5 bln - CLP.
newsitem.headline: Black Point delay could cost over HK$1.5 bln - CLP.

text.p: China Light & Power Co Ltd said on Tuesday that a deferral of the construction of its Black Point power station could cost from HK$200 million to more than HK$1.5 billion in additional costs.

The Hong Kong government asked China Light last November to submit a report on the costs of deferring units five to eight of the plant after a consultant's report recommended a halt or delay in the commissioning of four of the plant's eight units due to slow growth in electricity demand.

"We have calculated all the net present values of all these additional costs and it ranged between HK$0.2 billion to more than HK$1.5 billion under different scenarios," Katherine Ma, assistant public affairs manager at China Light, told Reuters.
She said the utility company had calculated different scenarios ranging from a three year deferral to five years for varying numbers of units.
Black Point consists of eight 312-megawatt units, two of which were commissioned in mid-1996 and two due to be switched on in mid-1997.
"Units five and six, basically they cannot be undone because unit five is already on the Black Point site and unit six is in the process of manufacturing," said Ma.

"Units seven and eight, which should be commissioned by the year 2000 and 2001, can be deferred physically. However, the information as provided by suppliers and lenders reveal that economically it is not justified to defer them," she added.
Ma said China Light's cost assessment was based on discussions with equipment suppliers and financial institutions.
She said while deferral would lead to short-term savings, the company would face additional costs in the long run.
The company has submitted alternative proposals for capacity reduction for the government to consider.

One would be to transfer power to Hongkong Electric Holdings Ltd, although this would involve complex commercial negotiations, said Ma. "At the end of the day, if it is materialised, it will have economic benefits to customers."
The other alternative would be for China Light to decommission some of the gas turbines at its Tsing Yi power station and Castle Peak power station, Ma added.
"It would have a very immediate effect of reducing the reserve margin by ten percent," she said.
While China Light has installed capacity of 7,500 megawatts, maximum demand is currently at 4,998, said Ma. The gas turbines constitute part of the installed capacity.
